Recursion is a programming technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself to break the task down into smaller, more manageable pieces. Each time the function calls itself, it works on a slightly simpler version of the original problem, moving closer to a final answer. To prevent the program from looping forever, the function must include a "base case," which is a specific condition that tells it when to stop calling itself. Once that stopping point is reached, the results from all the nested function calls bubble back up and combine to solve the original, larger problem.
